answer:
Treat the contract as a versioned structured document with stable clause IDs. Retrieve the applicable rule set and authoritative source passages, then run a verification stage that produces clause-specific findings: violated rule, evidence span, severity, and proposed remedy. A separate editing stage emits a bounded patch against those clause IDs rather than rewriting the entire document.

Validate that the patch applies to the expected document version, preserves protected clauses and defined terms, and does not silently change unrelated amounts, dates, parties, or cross-references. Re-run affected rules and produce a redline showing every change with its source citation. Rule conflicts and unsupported interpretations go to a reviewer. Approval must be bound to the actual patch/document version, not a vague instruction to accept future edits.

A generative model cannot guarantee zero hallucinated clauses. For constrained cases, approved clause templates and deterministic substitution can provide stronger guarantees about allowed text; otherwise require human review and abstain on missing authority. Measure false negatives on known violations, citation correctness, unauthorized edits, and reviewer acceptance. Never equate an automated compliance score with legal correctness.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** A clause-level result should link $(clause\_id,rule\_id,evidence\_span,proposed\_patch)$ so a reviewer can inspect the reasoning and change separately. Test patch locality and document invariants as well as finding precision/recall. This is an engineering workflow for review assistance; compliance conclusions depend on the applicable authoritative rules and qualified review. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) and [2](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents).
